videos.title: Titration Practical: Standard Solutions, Burette Technique and Errors | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson14.sa

Two benches titrate the same hydrochloric acid and both get concordant titres, yet their answers differ. Make a sodium carbonate standard, pipette the aliquot, set up and read the burette, run a rough titration then accurate ones to the first permanent orange, deal with a run spoiled by an air bubble, and calculate the acid's concentration. Then trace an error through the titre to the answer, and judge validity, reliability and accuracy. Includes a risk assessment and two exam-style questions.

0:43 Prepare the sodium carbonate standard
1:09 Make to the mark and calculate concentration
1:33 Measure the aliquot
2:01 Set up the burette
2:19 Read the meniscus and avoid parallax
2:49 Rough and accurate titrations
3:12 Select and average reliable titres
3:40 Calculate the unknown acid concentration
4:10 Trace the water-rinsed burette error
4:41 Keep the conditions controlled
4:57 Validity, reliability and accuracy
5:19 Assess the risks
5:45 Practice 1: a water-rinsed pipette
6:14 Answer 1: follow the smaller titre
6:38 Practice 2: rinsing the conical flask
7:04 Answer 2: extra carbonate
7:27 A titration you can trust
7:44 Key notes

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 6, Acid/Base Reactions. This video explains and analyses the practical; watching does not replace conducting a supervised investigation.

Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 6):
"conduct practical investigations to analyse the concentration of an unknown acid or base by titration"

Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: How does direct titration reveal an unknown concentration? Next: Standardisation and titration calculation practice.

videos.title: Strong Acid and Base pH: Dilution and Mixing Practice Questions | Year 12 Chemistry Module 6
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson11.sa

Practise four HSC-style pH questions on strong acids and bases. Find the pH of a dilute nitric acid solution and the hydroxide in it; dilute hydrochloric acid in a volumetric flask and check the change on the log scale; mix an acid and a base given only their pH values; and mix barium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid without forgetting the second hydroxide. Pause and try each question, then work through it step by step, with the right number of decimal places and a sense check at the end. Questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

videos.title: Weak Acid pH, Ka and Amphiprotic Ions: HSC-Style Practice Questions | Year 12 Chemistry Module 6
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson12.sa

Practise four HSC-style weak acid questions, and choose the method from the data. Find the pH of hypochlorous acid with the square-root shortcut and justify it; see the 5% check fail for chloroethanoic acid and solve the full equation; work backwards from a measured pH to Ka and pKa for benzoic acid; and write the reactions with water, then compare Ka with Kb to decide whether the hydrogen carbonate and dihydrogen phosphate ions mainly donate or accept a proton, and so whether baking soda and potassium dihydrogen phosphate give basic or acidic solutions. Pause and try each question, then work through it step by step. Questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

1:02 Use the square-root estimate
1:30 Check the approximation
1:52 Classic mistake: treating a weak acid as strong
2:06 Question 2: chloroethanoic acid pH
2:39 When the five per cent check fails
3:07 Solve the full equilibrium equation
3:38 Classic mistake: keeping a failed shortcut
3:53 Question 3: find Ka from measured pH
4:26 Work backwards to the equilibrium concentrations
4:53 Calculate Ka and pKa
5:18 Classic mistake: using the initial concentration
5:34 Question 4: amphiprotic ions
6:11 Does hydrogen carbonate mainly accept or donate?
6:47 Compare Ka and Kb for dihydrogen phosphate

7:40 Choose the method from the data
8:10 Key notes

- sodium hydrogen carbonate

videos.title: UV and Yeast Survival: Fair Tests, Relative Survival and Colony Counts | Year 12 Biology Module 6
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson02.sa

After two minutes of UV, a yeast plate grows five colonies instead of 142. So did UV make mutants? Work through a teacher-prepared UV and yeast dataset: what a colony means, why mutants hide among the survivors, the fair test and its lamp-off control, replicate plates, relative survival and a graph of every plate. Then see what the data support, how mutation would actually be measured, and how to judge validity, reliability and accuracy. Includes a risk assessment for UVC and microbial cultures, and two exam-style questions.

0:00 Do fewer colonies prove more mutation?
0:25 What a colony tells you
0:50 Four possible cell outcomes
1:22 Teacher-prepared data and UV safety
1:43 Design a fair comparison
2:09 Keep the lamp-off control comparable
2:28 Replicate plates and calculate means
2:51 Calculate relative survival
3:11 Plot every plate and the means
3:34 What the survival data support
3:55 What evidence would measure mutation?
4:21 Validity, reliability and accuracy
4:52 Assess the risks
5:21 Practice 1: evaluate a conclusion
5:54 Answer 1
6:17 Practice 2: evaluate a control
6:53 Answer 2
7:19 Colonies count survivors, changed or not
7:44 Key notes

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 6, Genetic Change. This video supports the electromagnetic-radiation aspect through survival data analysis; it does not cover every listed mutagen.

Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 6):
"explain how a range of mutagens operate, including but not limited to:
- electromagnetic radiation sources
- chemicals
- naturally occurring mutagens"

Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: How do mutagens increase DNA damage? Next: How can one base change affect a protein?
